title: Artist Identity: Name, Story & Visual Brand
skill: Define your artist name, story and visual brand into a consistent identity across every platform.
content:
Why identity is leverage, not vanity

A brand is the shortcut a promoter, a label A&R, or a stranger scrolling at 1am uses to decide whether you are worth their attention before they ever hear a note. It is the sum of your name, your story and your visuals — and the only thing that matters is whether it is consistent and legible. A scattered identity makes you forgettable; a focused one makes you bookable.

Choosing a name that survives a search

Your name is a database key. Before you commit, run the checks below — in this order, because failing any one of them can cost you months of momentum later.

  • Uniqueness: search the exact name on Google, Spotify, SoundCloud, Instagram and Bandcamp. If an established act already holds it in electronic music, pick again. Two artists sharing a name split streams, get cross-tagged and confuse promoters.
  • Handle availability: you want the same handle on Instagram, TikTok, SoundCloud and YouTube. If the exact handle is taken, a single consistent suffix (e.g. _music or dj) beats four different handles.
  • Spellability and say-ability: a name a club MC cannot pronounce or a fan cannot spell into a search bar is a tax on every booking. Avoid silent letters, accented characters and numbers-as-letters.
  • Trademark and genre fit: a deep-house alias that sounds like a hardcore act creates a mismatch the moment someone hears your music.
Lock it down the day you choose it. Register every handle, the .com if you can, and a Gmail in the name — even platforms you will not use for a year. Squatting your own name costs nothing now and is expensive to reclaim later.

Story: the one sentence and the paragraph

Your story is not your life. It is a positioning statement that tells someone what to expect. Build two versions and keep them everywhere identical.

  1. The one-liner (under 12 words): genre + flavour + a hook. Example shape: "London-based selector blending dub-techno and broken beat." This is your Instagram bio, your booking-email subject context, your MC intro.
  2. The bio paragraph (60-120 words, third person): what you play, where you have played or released, and what makes the sound distinct. Third person because that is what promoters paste into event listings.

Write to the listener's benefit, not your feelings. "I have been passionate about music since I was a kid" is invisible — every DJ says it. "Known for hour-long all-vinyl warm-ups that never break 122 BPM" is a brand.

Visual brand: the system, not the logo

Consistency beats polish. A simple identity applied everywhere reads as more professional than a beautiful logo used once.

ElementSpec to lockWhy it matters
WordmarkOne typeface for your name, used on every flyer and coverRecognition at thumbnail size
Colour palette2-3 hex codes maxFeed and covers read as one body of work
Press photoOne landscape, one portrait, high-res, neutralPromoters need both orientations
Profile imageIdentical across all platformsA fan recognises you mid-scroll

Apply it everywhere, then freeze it

Use the identical profile photo, the identical bio, the same handle and the same wordmark on Instagram, SoundCloud, Mixcloud, YouTube, Spotify for Artists and your EPK. When someone finds you on one platform and looks for you on another, the match should be instant. Then stop fiddling. Brand equity is built by repetition; redesigning every three months resets your recognition to zero. Revisit the visual system once a year at most, and only when your music has genuinely moved.
exercise: Lock your name and one-liner today. Run your chosen name through Google, Spotify, SoundCloud and Instagram to confirm it is clear, then register the matching handle on all four platforms. Write a 10-word one-liner and a 90-word third-person bio, and paste both, identical, into every profile.

title: Social Media & Content Strategy for DJs
skill: Build a content strategy that suits DJs and posts consistently without burning out.
content:
The DJ's content problem

Most DJs post only when they have a gig, then vanish for three weeks. The algorithm punishes the gaps, and a feed of nothing-but-flyers gives a stranger no reason to follow. The fix is not posting more — it is posting a small, repeatable set of formats that you can produce in batches.

Pick platforms by what they reward

PlatformBest for DJsCadence
InstagramReels of mixing clips, gig photos, Stories for behind-the-scenes3-4 posts/week, daily Stories
TikTokShort transition clips, track-ID reactions, discovery for new fans4-7 short clips/week
YouTubeFull mixes, studio breakdowns (long-tail search)1-2/month
SoundCloud / MixcloudThe mixes themselves (the calling card)1-2/month

You do not need all of them. Pick one short-form platform (Instagram or TikTok) plus one home for long mixes (SoundCloud, Mixcloud or YouTube). Two done well beats five done badly.

The three content buckets

Plan around buckets, not individual posts. Aim for a rough split so the feed is never all-promo.

  • Skill / craft (40%): a 30-second clip of a clean transition, a hot-cue trick, a track you are obsessed with this week. This proves you can actually DJ and is the most shareable.
  • Personality / behind-the-scenes (40%): crate digging, soundcheck, the drive home, a record-store haul. This is what turns followers into fans — people support people, not flyers.
  • Promo / proof (20%): upcoming gigs, a released mix, a label premiere. Because the other 80% earned attention, the promo actually lands.
The hook is the first 1.5 seconds. On Reels and TikTok, nobody reads your caption first. Start mid-action — the build before a drop, the moment hands hit the mixer. No slow intros, no logos. Earn the next two seconds, then the next.

Capture once, post for a month

The reason DJs burn out is they treat each post as a fresh production. Don't. Every time you play — at home or out — set a phone on a small tripod and record 10-15 minutes of close-up hands and the booth. From one session you can cut six to ten short clips. Batch the capture, batch the editing, then schedule. A two-hour Sunday session can fill two weeks.

Practical capture settings

  • Film vertical (9:16) for Reels/TikTok; keep a horizontal angle too if you want YouTube.
  • Get the phone close to the jog wheels and faders — hands are the visual story.
  • Record clean audio off the booth or a line-out where you can; phone-mic-in-a-club audio is muddy and copyright-flagged. Many DJs replace clip audio with the clean recording of the same mix.

Consistency over virality

One viral clip you cannot repeat is luck. Three posts a week for a year is a brand. Set a realistic floor — say three short clips and two Stories a week — and protect it like a gig. Use a scheduler so a busy week does not break the streak. Reply to every comment in the first hour; early engagement is what the algorithm reads as "show this to more people." Track which formats actually drive saves and follows, do more of those, and quietly drop what doesn't.
exercise: Batch a week of content from one session. Next time you mix, film 10 minutes of close-up hands vertically with clean line-out audio. Cut three 20-30 second clips — each starting mid-build with no intro — label them craft, personality and promo, and schedule one every other day.

title: Recorded Mixes as Your Calling Card
skill: Record and publish a standout mix on SoundCloud, Mixcloud or YouTube that wins you bookings.
content:
The mix is your demo, CV and portfolio in one

When a promoter is deciding whether to book you, they will not come to your bedroom — they will press play on a mix. A great recorded set is the single highest-leverage asset you can make. It has to do two jobs at once: prove you can mix cleanly, and prove you have taste and a story.

Concept before record button

The mixes that travel have an angle, not just a tracklist. Decide before you start: a 60-minute deep-house sunset journey, a high-energy 30-minute peak-time showcase, a label or genre tribute. A focused 30-minute mix beats a meandering two-hour one for getting booked — promoters and A&Rs rarely listen past the first few minutes, so front-load your strongest material and tightest mixing in the opening five minutes.

Length and structure

  • Booking demo: 30-45 min. One clear energy arc — establish, build, peak, resolve.
  • Mixcloud/podcast series: 60 min, consistent length so subscribers know what to expect.
  • Plan the arc on paper: where the first big moment lands (around 8-10 min), where the peak sits (two-thirds in), how you land it.

Recording clean

Record the master off the mixer's record-out (USB or RCA REC OUT), not a room mic. Capture into your DAW or the recorder at 44.1kHz/24-bit if possible. Set your gain so peaks sit around -6 dB to leave headroom — a clipped recording sounds amateur instantly and cannot be fixed.

StepSetting / action
SourceMixer REC OUT or audio-interface line input, not a mic
LevelsMaster peaks ~-6 dB, no red clip lights
FormatWAV/AIFF 44.1kHz, mix down to 320kbps MP3 for upload
LoudnessLight master limiter to ~-9 to -7 LUFS; do not crush it
Do it in one take, but allow yourself takes. A live one-take feels human and is what bookers want to hear. But there is no prize for keeping a take with a trainwreck in it — if you stumble in the first version, record it again. Just do not edit individual transitions together so heavily that it stops sounding like a real DJ set.

Where to publish

  • Mixcloud: fully licensed, so full-track DJ mixes stay up without copyright strikes. The default for radio-style and long mixes. Tracklists are credited automatically.
  • SoundCloud: great for reach and reposts in the underground scene, but unlicensed full-track mixes can be muted or removed. Best for shorter mixes, edits and original work.
  • YouTube: huge discovery via search, but the strictest copyright system — long DJ mixes often get claimed (revenue goes to rights holders) or blocked. Good for visual sets and originals.

Packaging that earns the click

The audio is only half the job. Give the mix cover art in your brand colours and wordmark, a clear title (Artist Name — Series #04 [Deep House]), a full tracklist (promoters check whether you actually have the records), and a two-line description with the concept. Pin it. Then seed it: send it directly to a handful of promoters and DJs you respect rather than just posting and praying. A targeted message — "new 35-min deep-house mix, thought of your night" — beats a public broadcast every time.
exercise: Record a 30-minute calling-card mix in one take. Plan a single energy arc on paper, record off the mixer's REC OUT with peaks near -6 dB, and put your strongest two transitions in the first five minutes. Upload to Mixcloud with branded art, a full tracklist and a two-line concept, then DM it to three promoters.

tracks.title: Music Sounds Better with You
tracks.why: A long, loopy, instantly recognisable groove that makes a strong, mixable opening statement for a calling-card mix.

tracks.title: Untitled (How Does It Feel)
tracks.artist: Floating Points (or any long deep cut)
tracks.why: Extended evolving arrangement to practice building an energy arc rather than just mixing track-to-track.

title: Live Streaming on Twitch/YouTube: Setup, Audio & Growth
skill: Set up a clean live-stream audio chain and grow an audience streaming sets on Twitch or YouTube.
content:
Why stream, and the audio reality

Streaming turns practice time into audience-building. The single thing that separates a watchable stream from an unwatchable one is audio — viewers forgive a cheap camera but leave instantly on muddy, clipping, or out-of-sync sound. Get the audio chain right first.

The clean audio chain

Never let your camera or phone mic capture the room. Send the mixer's master directly into your computer.

  1. Mixer to interface: take the mixer's REC OUT or BOOTH/MASTER out via RCA or USB into an audio interface (or a mixer with a built-in USB audio interface — most DJM and modern controllers have this).
  2. Set levels: in your streaming software, your master should peak around -6 dB to leave headroom. Watch the meter, not your ears.
  3. Mic (optional): if you talk, use a separate USB/XLR mic on its own channel so you can duck the music under your voice.
  4. Monitor: wear headphones fed from the stream return so you hear exactly what viewers hear and can catch sync drift or silence.
SoftwareBest forNote
OBS StudioFull control, free, scenes/overlaysThe standard; steeper learning curve
StreamlabsEasier overlays and alertsBuilt on OBS, more bloat
Twitch StudioQuick startLimited; fine to learn on

Encoding settings that don't buffer

  • Resolution/FPS: 1080p30 is plenty for a DJ stream; 720p30 if your upload is under ~5 Mbps.
  • Video bitrate: 3500-6000 kbps for 1080p30.
  • Audio bitrate: set as high as the platform allows — 160 kbps minimum, 256-320 kbps if possible. Music streams live or die on audio bitrate; do not leave it at the 128 default.
  • Encoder: hardware (NVENC/Apple) to spare your CPU for the audio.
Copyright is the streamer's landmine. Twitch and YouTube scan audio. YouTube will claim or mute copyrighted music aggressively; Twitch can issue DMCA strikes and mute your VOD. Stream your own edits, license-friendly catalogues, or accept that VODs may be muted. Many DJs stream live (lower risk than a saved VOD) and delete or disable the recording afterward.

Scene and overlay basics

Build one clean scene: camera on you/the decks, a small overlay with your handle and socials, and ideally a now-playing or simple visual. Add a "starting soon" and "be right back" scene. Keep it uncluttered — the gear and your hands are the show.

Growth: consistency and the schedule

Streaming rewards regularity more than any other platform. The algorithm and your viewers both reward a fixed slot.

  • Pick a fixed day and time and stream it every week without fail, even to two viewers. Tell people when you go live.
  • Stream length: 1.5-2 hours gives the discovery systems time to surface you and viewers time to arrive.
  • Engage live: read chat by name, take requests, talk between tracks. Interaction is the entire reason someone chooses a stream over a polished recorded mix.
  • Cross-promote: clip the best 30 seconds for Reels/TikTok to pull new viewers back to the stream (ties directly to your content strategy).
  • Network in: raid and host other DJs, get raided back, guest on each other's streams. The streaming scene grows by collaboration, not solo grind.

Monetisation (subs, Bits, channel memberships, tips) follows audience — do not chase it early. Build the room first; the revenue is covered in the business course.
exercise: Run a 20-minute test stream before going public. Route your mixer's REC OUT into an interface and into OBS, set audio to 256 kbps and master peaks near -6 dB, and add a basic overlay with your handle. Stream privately, watch the VOD on headphones, and confirm there is no clipping, no sync drift and no silence.

title: The EPK & Sending Demos to Labels & Promoters
skill: Assemble an EPK and send targeted demos to labels and promoters that actually get opened.
content:
What an EPK is and why you need one

An Electronic Press Kit is a single link that gives a promoter or label everything they need to say yes, in under two minutes of their time. Bookers are busy; if the answer to "who is this, what do they play, can they actually mix, and what will they look like on my flyer" is not instantly available, they move on. The EPK exists to remove every reason to scroll past you.

The EPK checklist

ElementDetail
BioOne-liner + 90-word third-person paragraph (from your brand work)
Best mixOne standout 30-45 min set, embedded and front-and-centre
Press photosHigh-res, one landscape + one portrait, downloadable
Music/releasesLinks to originals, edits or notable mixes
Past gigs/proofNotable venues, support slots, residencies, radio
Tech riderWhat you need to play (CDJs, mixer, etc.)
Socials + contactBooking email and follower counts if respectable

Host it on a simple one-page site or a free EPK tool. One link, mobile-friendly, with a downloadable photo pack. Keep it to a single scrollable page — nobody clicks through tabs.

Sending a demo to a label

A demo is not an EPK; it is one or two of your best original tracks, sent the way the label asks. The most common reason demos get ignored is ignoring the submission rules.

  1. Target, don't spray. Pick labels whose recent releases actually sound like your track. A techno demo to a deep-house label is an instant delete and burns the relationship.
  2. Follow their channel. Many labels have a demo form, a specific email, or explicitly say "no unsolicited demos." Respect it exactly. Sending a SoundCloud link when they want WAV via a form gets you binned.
  3. Private streaming link. Send a private SoundCloud or unlisted link, not a 50MB attachment. Let them stream first; send files only if asked.
  4. Lead with the music. Two sentences: who you are, why this track fits this label (reference a recent release), and the link. That is the whole email.
The subject line decides if it gets opened. Use something specific and honest: "Demo — [Track Name] — Deep/Dub Techno — for [Label] consideration." Not "PLEASE LISTEN!!!" or "the next big hit." A&Rs filter by genre and professionalism in the inbox preview.

Pitching a promoter for a booking

Different goal, different message. The promoter wants to know you will fill the room and not be a headache.

  • Personalise: name the night, say why you fit their roster and crowd.
  • Lead with your best mix link and one line of proof (a venue, a residency, a draw).
  • Make the ask clear and small: "I would love to be considered for a warm-up slot." Junior, specific asks get yeses.
  • Keep it to a phone-screen length. No essays, no attachments.

The follow-up and the long game

One polite follow-up after 7-10 days is fine; a third is pestering. No reply usually means "not now," not "never." The DJs who get signed and booked are the ones whose name the gatekeeper has already seen — supporting the label's releases, attending the night, engaging genuinely for months before the ask. Warm beats cold every time. Send fewer, better, more-targeted messages; treat every gatekeeper as someone you might work with for a decade.
exercise: Build a one-page EPK and send one targeted demo. Assemble bio, your best 30-45 min mix, two press photos and contact into a single shareable link. Then pick one label whose recent releases genuinely match your track, find their stated submission method, and send a three-sentence pitch with a private stream link and a specific subject line.

title: Networking & Building a Local Scene and Online Community
skill: Build genuine relationships in your local scene and an engaged online community around your music.
content:
Careers are built on rooms, not algorithms

Almost every booking a working DJ gets traces back to a relationship — a promoter who knows them, a DJ who recommended them, a crew they are part of. Online reach matters, but the local scene is where bookings, residencies and the genuine support that sustains a career actually live. Network like a member of the community, not a salesperson.

Showing up in the local scene

  • Be a regular before you are a DJ. Go to the nights you want to play. Promoters book people they recognise from the dancefloor, not strangers in their DMs. Twenty nights attended buys more goodwill than a hundred cold messages.
  • Support other DJs publicly. Share their sets, show up for their sets, tag them honestly. The scene notices generosity and notices takers.
  • Bring value, not just asks. Offer to flyer, film the night, run the door, do a B2B warm-up. Being useful gets you in the room where bookings are decided.
  • Find or form a crew. Collectives throw their own parties, pool followings and book each other. A crew of five DJs each bringing 20 people is a viable night — and a reason promoters take all of you seriously.
Generosity compounds, transactional behaviour repels. Help people before you need anything. The DJ who supports others, shows up reliably and never makes it weird becomes the first name people think of when a slot opens. Reputation in a local scene travels faster than any flyer.

The etiquette that gets you re-booked

DoDon't
Play the slot you're given (warm-up = warm-up)Play peak-time bangers in the warm-up to show off
End on time, clean handoverRun over and crowd the next DJ
Thank the promoter and sound engineerVanish the second you finish
Bring people / share the eventExpect a room someone else filled

Most re-bookings are decided by behaviour, not just the set. A solid DJ who reads the slot, is easy to work with and helps fill the room beats a flashier one who is a headache.

Building the online community

An online community is the same principle at scale: relationships, not broadcasts. The goal is a small group of genuine fans, not a big number of passive followers.

  1. Reply to everyone early on. Every comment, every DM, by name. Early fans who feel seen become your evangelists.
  2. Give them a home. A Discord, a close-friends Story list, a newsletter, or a regular stream chat — somewhere the same people gather repeatedly and recognise each other. Community needs a room.
  3. Recurring rituals. A weekly stream, a monthly mix, a track-ID Friday. Predictable touchpoints turn followers into regulars.
  4. Connect them to each other, not just to you. The strongest communities are horizontal — fans who became friends through your music will stay for decades.

The 1000-true-fans mindset

You do not need to go viral. A few hundred people who genuinely care — who will buy a ticket, stream a mix, support a release, tell a friend — outvalue tens of thousands of passive scrollers. Build relationships deep, not just wide. Tie this back to everything else: your content gives people a reason to find you, your mixes prove you are worth following, and your scene and community turn that attention into the bookings, support and longevity that make a real career.
exercise: Do one genuine, non-transactional thing this week in each direction. Attend a local night you want to play and introduce yourself to the promoter as a fan with no ask. Then reply personally to every comment and DM on your last three posts, and message one DJ whose work you admire purely to say what you liked about their last set.
